meta.title: Pre-launch readiness and go-live
meta.lead: How a finished site on its netlify.app address becomes the client's live site on their own domain — audited, keyed, paid-path-tested, signed off and cut over. If you remember one thing: nothing is verified until you have seen it on the live domain, and nothing that touches money is done outside Claude Fable against a test key.

items.d: Takes a site that WEB-004 left complete on its *.netlify.app address and makes it ready to be a business: search and answer-engine ready, accessible to WCAG 2.2 AA, fast on every page, correct at every screen size, legally complete, wired to the client's live payment, email, booking and CRM accounts, proven with a test booking, approved by the client, and moved onto the client's real domain without taking their email down.

SEO and GEO. Accessibility to WCAG 2.2 AA. The Lighthouse loop. BrowserStack responsive checks. Legal and policy pages. The HGM and Meta client pixels. Collecting and installing the live keys — Stripe, Resend, the booking platform, GoHighLevel. The money path. A test booking and the booking-flow walk. The Resend check. Client sign-off. The DNS cutover. Confirming the site is live.
Everything WEB-004 covers — the build, the Resources folder, the forms, matching the original. Google Analytics 4, Search Console and Hotjar, which are WEB-003 and start the day the site is live.

blocks.text: This SOP starts at WEB-004 task 8.4: the pull request is merged, the team has reviewed the site in the client websites space, and the Asana task lists the keys still missing. It ends where WEB-003 phase 1 begins: the site answers on the client's domain and the repository can be proven to be the live site.

blocks.t: This is a field-test draft
blocks.text: Version 0.1 was built before the interview answers, the WCAG audit prompt and the promo-code campaign links document arrived. Every gap is marked [NEEDS INPUT] in place. Run the first launch against it, write down what actually happened at each flag, and hand the answers back — v0.2 clears them. Do not treat a flagged task as an instruction.

blocks.t: Six standing rules
blocks.d: These hold on every launch. Everything else in this document is procedure; these are not negotiable.

items.t: Money work happens in Claude Fable, against test keys, never a real charge
items.d: Anything that touches prices, coupons, the payment intent, checkout, webhooks or an API key is done in Claude Fable with Stripe in test mode. A live secret key never sits in .env.local on your machine and never appears in a prompt.

items.t: The client's email must survive the cutover
items.d: Before any DNS record changes, every existing MX, SPF, DKIM and DMARC record is written down; after the change a test message is sent to the client's own address and seen to arrive. A launch that breaks the client's inbox is a failed launch.

items.t: Nothing is verified until it has been seen on the live domain
items.d: A check passed on netlify.app, on a deploy preview or on localhost is a check that has to be repeated on https://<client-domain> after cutover. Phase 11 exists for this.

items.t: Every audit prompt's output is checked, not trusted
items.d: Claude reports "all pages 100/100" or "the site is AA"; you open the page and look. Each audit phase pairs the prompt with a by-hand check, and the by-hand check is the one that counts.

A key, a Location ID, a pixel ID, a domain record — it comes from the client's record in hgmportal.com, from 1Password, or from the client through their account manager. If it is not there, it is a named gap on the Asana task, never something typed in from another client.

items.t: The client approves before DNS moves
items.d: Written sign-off is recorded on the Asana task before phase 10 begins. No sign-off, no cutover, whatever the deadline says.

Every audit prompt, every fix, every commit. Claude Code runs here, and Claude Fable for phases 7 and 8.
The dig and curl checks in phases 10 and 11. Everything here also works from the VS Code terminal.
Prompts only. Everything that is a key, a record or a dashboard — Stripe, Resend, GoHighLevel, Netlify, the DNS host — is point and click in a browser.

blocks.t: Pick one route per task
blocks.text: Wherever a task can be done more than one way you will see a point-and-click box, a terminal box or a Claude prompt box. They do the same thing. Only routes that exist are offered; a task with one box has one route.

items.d: Making a site legible to AI answer engines the way SEO makes it legible to Google: structured data that says what each page is, and an llms.txt file at the site root describing the site in plain text.
JSON-LD blocks in a page's HTML describing the page's entity — a vacation rental, an organisation, an FAQ — in a vocabulary search and answer engines read. Checked with Google's Rich Results Test.

The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines at level AA, the standard phase 3 audits to: keyboard operability, text alternatives on images, colour contrast, visible focus, and the rest. [NEEDS INPUT: WCAG audit prompt — the criteria list it enumerates]
Google's page audit tool, scoring Performance, Accessibility, Best Practices and SEO out of 100. The loop in phase 4 runs it until every page scores 100 in every category.
Stripe's sandbox. Test keys begin pk_test_ and sk_test_; live keys begin pk_live_ and sk_live_. A charge made with a test key is not real. Every money task in this SOP happens in test mode.

A URL on the site that Stripe or the booking platform calls when something happens — a payment succeeds, a reservation is created. It is registered on their side with the site's address, and it has to be re-registered when that address changes at cutover.

The Meta pixel is browser-side tracking; the Conversions API (CAPI) reports the same events server-side. The CAPI token is one HGM value shared across clients. [NEEDS INPUT: Q19 — whether the pixel ID is per client or shared, and what the "HGM pixel" is]

The registrar is where the domain is owned and renewed; the DNS host is where its records are served. Often the same company, often not — Ridge & Falls was registered at Squarespace Domains with DNS at Cloudflare.

The record types a cutover touches. A and ALIAS point the bare domain at a server; CNAME points www at another name; MX routes email; TXT carries SPF, DKIM and DMARC, which are what stop the client's mail being marked as spam.
How long a DNS record is cached, in seconds. Lowering it before a cutover is what makes the change take effect quickly, and it has to be lowered before the old TTL has expired to make any difference.
The moment the domain's records stop pointing at the old site and start pointing at Netlify. The point of no return in this SOP; section 08 is its gate.

blocks.text: Phase 1 — Confirm the build is ready to be checked
blocks.d: Prove you are starting from the merged build, on a machine whose environment is filled, on a branch you can throw away.

blocks.t: Read the handoff on the Asana task
blocks.d: Open the Asana task and read the comment WEB-004 task 8.4 left: the netlify.app address, the list of keys still missing with a name against each, and the TOKENS.md total.
blocks.expect: You know which keys phase 6 has to collect before you open a single dashboard.

blocks.t: Pull main and confirm the deployed site is main
blocks.d: Fetch, fast-forward, then compare the commit Netlify has deployed with origin/main.
blocks.expect: git status -sb shows main...origin/main with no [behind N], and the deployed commit equals origin/main.

body.label: Terminal / CLI
body.text:
git fetch origin && git status -sb
git pull --ff-only
git rev-parse origin/main    # compare with the commit shown on the Netlify deploy

body.label: Claude prompt
body.text: Fetch origin and tell me how far behind main is. If a fast-forward is possible, pull. Then ask the Netlify connector for get-deploy-for-site on this site and tell me whether commit_ref equals origin/main. Make no changes.

blocks.t: Check .env.local is filled, by length
blocks.d: Print each key with the length of its value, never the value. If keys are blank, restore the file from the client's 1Password entry (HGM-SOP-WEB-001) and restart the dev server.
blocks.expect: Every key WEB-004 filled shows a non-zero length, and the blank ones are exactly the list from task 1.1.

body.label: Terminal / CLI
body.text: awk -F= '/^[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*=/ { print $1, length($2) }' .env.local

body.label: Claude prompt
body.text: Check .env.local: list every key with the LENGTH of its value. Never print a value. Tell me which keys are blank.

body.t: Never print or paste a value
body.text: Lengths, not contents. A value pasted into a chat, an Asana comment or a screenshot is a key that has to be rotated.

blocks.t: Make the pre-launch branch and open the cost row
blocks.d: Create a branch named pre-launch off main following HGM-SOP-WEB-002, and add today's row to TOKENS.md (WEB-004 task 3.4).
blocks.expect: Every audit fix in phases 2 to 5 lands on pre-launch and reaches production through one pull request in task 8.6.

body.label: Terminal / CLI
body.text: git checkout -b pre-launch

blocks.d: Give every page its titles, descriptions and social shares, then make the site legible to answer engines. The reference for voice and tone is the finished Paradise Pointe site.

blocks.t: Set meta titles, descriptions and social shares for every page
blocks.d: In Claude Code, run the prompt below with the Paradise Pointe URL and the master doc attached. [NEEDS INPUT: Q23 — the Paradise Pointe URL and the master doc's name and location]
blocks.expect: A list of every page with its title, description and share image. Compare the list against the sitemap; no page may be missing.

body.label: Claude prompt
body.text: Set the meta title, meta description and social share (Open Graph and Twitter card) for every page on this site. Use <Paradise Pointe URL> as the reference for a site that is already done, and read <master doc> to understand the voice and tone to write in. List every page and the values you set.
body.note: fill in the two angle-bracket values

blocks.t: Check the tags on three pages yourself
blocks.d: Open the home page, the listings page and one property page on the deploy preview. View source and find <title>, <meta name="description", og:title, og:description and og:image on each.
blocks.expect: Every tag is present and the share image URL loads. A title that reads as a template placeholder is a fail.

body.label: Point & click
body.text: Browser: View Page Source (Cmd + Option + U in Chrome) → Cmd + F "og:image".

body.label: Terminal / CLI
body.text: curl -s https://<deploy-preview>/ | grep -o '<meta property="og:[a-z:]*" content="[^"]*"'
(image to be added) — One page's rendered <head> showing the title, description and social tags.

blocks.t: Run the GEO audit — schema and llms.txt
blocks.d: In Claude Code, run the prompt below.
blocks.expect: JSON-LD on every page type, one builder function per entity (WEB-003 task 7.2 explains why), and llms.txt at the site root.

body.label: Claude prompt
body.text: Do a full GEO audit of this site. Optimise the site for generative engines: add schema where it is missing so that each page's entity is described, update existing schema so LLMs know what each page is about, and create an llms.txt file at the site root describing the site, its pages and its properties. Fill schema only from data the site actually has; leave out anything you would have to invent. List every change.

blocks.t: Check the schema and read llms.txt
blocks.d: Run Google's Rich Results Test on the listings page first, then one property page. Open https://<deploy-preview>/llms.txt and read it.
blocks.expect: Zero critical issues on both pages, and llms.txt describes this client and no other.

body.t: Test the list page, not just the detail page
body.text: On Ridge & Falls the listings page emitted a thin copy of each property with the same @id as the full node on the property page, and the test scored every cabin "2 critical". The list page is where it shows.

blocks.t: Commit and push
blocks.d: Commit the SEO and GEO changes on pre-launch and push. Netlify rebuilds the deploy preview.
blocks.expect: The preview carries the new tags and task 2.2's checks pass against it.

body.label: Terminal / CLI
body.text: git add -A && git commit -m "feat: SEO meta, schema and llms.txt" && git push -u origin pre-launch

blocks.d: Run the audit prompt, answer its questions, then check the site by hand against the criteria.

blocks.t: Run the accessibility audit prompt
blocks.d: In Claude Code, paste the prompt exactly as written.
blocks.expect: A list of issues found and fixed, and a list of questions.

body.label: Claude prompt
body.text: Do a quick accessibility check as in an audit on the website and correct all the accessibility issues. Ask questions if you are unsure. Ensure the website is keyboard navigable, AA rated where possible, add alt tags to all images and anything else that needs to be done to enhance accessibility.

blocks.t: Answer every question before letting it continue
blocks.d: The prompt says "ask questions if you are unsure" — read them. A typical one is what a decorative image's alt text should be, or whether a client colour that fails contrast may be changed.
blocks.expect: No question is left unanswered, and no brand colour has been changed without the client's say.

body.t: Keep the client's swatches even when contrast fails
body.text: Do not let the audit silently change a brand colour. Document the contrast ratio at the declaration and tell the account manager the passing alternative, so the client decides. WEB-003 section 06 records the same rule.

blocks.t: Check keyboard navigation and alt text yourself
blocks.d: On the deploy preview, put the mouse down. Tab from the top of the home page through the search widget, into the listings, onto a property page and into the booking form. Then confirm no image on the listings page lacks an alt attribute.
blocks.expect: You can reach and operate every control with the keyboard, focus is visible at every step, and the grep prints nothing.

body.label: Terminal / CLI
body.text: curl -s https://<deploy-preview>/listings | grep -o '<img[^>]*>' | grep -v 'alt='

body.label: Point & click
body.text:
Browser: click in the address bar, then press Tab repeatedly.
Watch for the focus ring on every link, button and field.
Press Enter on the search button; keep tabbing into the results.
(image to be added) — The site with a keyboard focus ring visible on a button, proving the indicator is not clipped. Ring the focus ring.

blocks.t: Check the remaining WCAG 2.2 AA criteria
blocks.d: [NEEDS INPUT: WCAG audit prompt — the criteria list, the check for each, and the pass condition. This task becomes a table once the audit prompt is supplied.]
blocks.expect: Every criterion in the table passes or has a named exception on the Asana task.

blocks.d: Two loops, each followed by a look.

blocks.t: Run the Lighthouse loop
blocks.d: In Claude Code, run the prompt below. [NEEDS INPUT: Q20 and Q21 — whether the loop runs against localhost, the deploy preview or production; Lighthouse via the CLI, DevTools or a Netlify plugin; whether 100/100 means all four categories; and the accepted floor if the loop cannot get there]
blocks.expect: A per-page table of the four scores, all 100.

body.label: Claude prompt
body.text: Next create a loop that checks Lighthouse and continues to loop until everything and every page is 100/100.

body.t: A loop is blunt here too
body.text: WEB-004 warns that a matching loop stops improving while still spending tokens. A Lighthouse loop is safer because the score is a hard number, but if it has run for [NEEDS INPUT: Q21 — a time or pass limit] without reaching 100, stop it and fix the remaining items by name.
(image to be added) — A Lighthouse run on the home page showing the four scores at the end of the loop. Ring the Performance score.

blocks.t: Run Lighthouse yourself on three pages
blocks.d: In Chrome, open DevTools, choose the Lighthouse panel, and run the home page, the listings page and one property page — mobile and desktop.
blocks.expect: The scores you see match the table Claude reported. If they do not, the loop measured a different build — see section 07.

body.text: A Lighthouse run showing the four 100s. Crop to the four score circles and the page URL; ring the Performance score.

blocks.t: Run the responsive check on BrowserStack
blocks.d: In Claude Code, run the prompt below. [NEEDS INPUT: Q22 — how Claude reaches BrowserStack (an MCP, or you drive it), and the device list HGM tests against]

body.label: Claude prompt
body.text: Check mobile responsiveness on BrowserStack, all breakpoints on the website and all device sizes should be perfect.
(image to be added) — The BrowserStack device grid part-way through a responsive pass.

blocks.t: Look at it on a real phone
blocks.d: Open the deploy preview on your own phone. Walk home, listings, property, the booking form. Open the mobile menu and the pop-up.
blocks.expect: Nothing overflows, nothing is cut off, the sticky search widget behaves, and the pop-up fits the screen. BrowserStack emulates; a phone is the truth.

body.label: Claude prompt — Fable
body.text: The Stripe publishable and secret test keys have been added. Register the webhooks for both the booking platform and Stripe. The Supabase access token has been added. body.text: Claude can only confirm a key by making a call with it. Read what it did: a Resend key is confirmed by a sent test email you can see in Resend's log, a GHL key by a contact appearing in the sub-account, a Meta key by a test event. If it says "the key looks valid" without a call, it did not check.

Every audit checked by hand, not only reported by Claude: tags (2.2), schema (2.4), keyboard and alt (3.3), Lighthouse (4.2), a real phone (4.4).
Privacy policy and terms of use reachable from the footer; the cancellation policy identical on property page, confirmation and email.
Every variable in ENV.template set on Netlify; .env.local saved to the client's 1Password vault; no key beginning sk_live_ on any HGM machine.
Webhooks registered for Stripe and the booking platform, and a delivered event seen for the test payment.
Test booking made, confirmation email seen delivered in Resend, reservation seen in the booking platform and cancelled, contact seen in GoHighLevel.
Client's written approval pasted into the Asana task, with the cutover time and the client contact for the day.
Registrar and DNS host known; every existing record captured to 1Password; MX and TXT records listed.
DNS access confirmed, or the person making the change booked for the window.
TTL lowered and the old TTL expired.
Both domains added in Netlify Domain management; redirect map in place and three redirects tested.
Rollback written down: which records to restore, and the old host still running.
A second person watching, if this is your first cutover.
